summary: This note explains rifts in geology: linear zones where the lithosphere is pulled apart through extensional tectonics, typically forming graben or half-graben structures. It covers rift geometry and accommodation zones, the stages of rift development from initiation to break-up and seafloor spreading, magmatism, the economic importance of rifts for minerals and hydrocarbons, and a list of example rifts worldwide.
one_line: Overview of geological rifts: extensional zones where lithosphere is pulled apart, their geometry, development to break-up, magmatism, resources, and examples.
key_facts: In geology, a rift is a linear zone where the lithosphere is being pulled apart, an example of extensional tectonics.
Typical rift features are a central linear downfaulted depression called a graben, or more commonly a half-graben with normal faulting and rift-flank uplifts mainly on one side.
Major rifts occur along the central axis of most mid-ocean ridges, where new oceanic crust and lithosphere is created along a divergent plate boundary.
Failed rifts typically develop at a triple junction where three converging rifts meet over a hotspot; the third ultimately fails, becoming an aulacogen.
Segment lengths of rifts vary with the elastic thickness of the lithosphere: the Baikal Rift has segment lengths in excess of 80 km, while in warmer thin lithosphere they may be less than 30 km.
Accommodation zones are segment boundary zones that generally cross the rift axis at a high angle and accommodate differences in fault displacement between segments.
Rift shoulders are typically about 70 km wide.
Elevated passive continental margins such as the Brazilian Highlands, the Scandinavian Mountains and India's Western Ghats are not rift shoulders, contrary to what was previously thought.
The amount of post-rift subsidence is related to the beta factor, defined as initial crustal thickness divided by final crustal thickness.
The North Sea rift shows evidence of several separate rift phases from the Permian through to the Earliest Cretaceous, a period of over 100 million years.
Alkali basalts and bimodal volcanism are common products of rift-related magmatism.
SedEx mineral deposits are found mainly in continental rift settings and form within post-rift sequences when hydrothermal fluids associated with magmatic activity are expelled at the seabed.
Thirty percent of giant oil and gas fields are found within continental rift settings.
In 1999 it was estimated that there were 200 billion barrels of recoverable oil reserves hosted in rifts.
Just over half of estimated oil reserves are found in rifts containing marine syn-rift and post-rift sequences.
The bottom of Lake Baikal is the deepest continental rift on the earth.
